$$

Suppose a particle $P$ is initially at the point $(1,0)$ and moves counterclockwise along the unit circle with a fixed **angular velocity** of $\dfrac\pi3$ **radians per second.** 

The first three seconds of the particle's motion are illustrated below.

![](images/00/009b83d5d0e48c6983950a48523838cc569b3a92511dc9362630316b1d88f86b.png)

    

Since the angular velocity is constant, we refer to this as **uniform circular motion**. This fixed angular velocity is denoted $\omega,$ and we write

$$
\omega = \dfrac\pi 3\,\textrm{rad/s}.
$$

Now, let $\mathbf r(t)$ be the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$ Then, we have

$$
\mathbf {r}(t)= \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right) \, \mathbf i + \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right) \,\mathbf j.
$$

It's worth building a picture of why this formula is true:

- We know that $\mathbf r(\theta) = \cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j$ traces out a unit circle, starting at the point $(1,0).$

- We can see from the picture that $P$ will return to the starting position after $t=6$ seconds, so the angular frequency of the motion is

$$
\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi t}{3})\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi t}{3})\,j\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $P$ indeed returns to its starting location when $t=6{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(6) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{6\pi }{3})\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{6\pi }{3})\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)\,j \\  & =r(0).\end{aligned}
$$

In general, if a particle moves counterclockwise along a circle of radius $R$ centered at $O$ with initial position $(R,0),$ then its position vector $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\mathbf {r}(t)= R\left(\cos\omega t \, \mathbf i + \sin\omega t \,\mathbf j\right)\!\,.
$$

Note that for clockwise motion, we have $\omega < 0.$

Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173205 :tutorial/content "Suppose a particle $P$ moves along a circle of radius $R$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. 

![](images/45/4564f4c4fcd8068f3bf1645a310afab7fcdc2f82fec6966cb220558c1e93639a.png)

    

Note the following:

- The **position vector** $\mathbf r$ extends from the origin to $P$ in the *radial* direction, while

- the **velocity vector** $\mathbf v$ points in the direction of the particle's motion, *tangential* to the circle.

First, let's assume that $P$ is at the point $(R,0)$ when $t=0.$ Then, we have

$$
\mathbf r(t) = R\left(\cos\omega t \, \mathbf i + \sin\omega t \,\mathbf j\right).
$$

We can easily derive a convenient formula relating $\mathbf v$ and $\omega$ by differentiating $\mathbf r(t){:}$

Differentiating once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & ={r}^{′}(t) \\  & ={(R(\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\,j))}^{′} \\  & =R\omega (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\,j).\end{aligned}
$$

By computing the magnitude of this vector, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}||v|{|}^{2} & ={R}^{2}{\omega }^{2}((-\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t)^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t)}^{2}) \\  & ={R}^{2}{\omega }^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡\omega t+{cos}^{2}⁡\omega t) \\  & ={R}^{2}{\omega }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Taking the square root, we get

$$
||\mathbf v || = R|\omega|.
$$

Note that while the magnitude of the velocity vector (i.e., the speed) is constant, its direction is continuously changing, which means that an object in uniform circular motion also experiences *acceleration* (more on this shortly)." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173260 :tutorial/content "Let's return to our particle $P$ moving along a circle of radius $R$ centered at the origin in the $xy$ plane. 

![](images/45/4564f4c4fcd8068f3bf1645a310afab7fcdc2f82fec6966cb220558c1e93639a.png)

    

Once again, let's assume that $P$ is at the point $(R,0)$ when $t=0.$ Then, we have

$$
\mathbf r(t) = R\left(\cos\omega t \, \mathbf i + \sin\omega t \,\mathbf j\right).
$$

Differentiating, we get the velocity vector $\mathbf v{:}$ 

$$
\mathbf v(t) =R\omega\left(-\sin\omega t \, \mathbf i + \cos\omega t \,\mathbf j\right)
$$

Differentiating once more, we get an expression for the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & ={v}^{′}(t) \\  & =R\omega {(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\,j)}^{′} \\  & =R\omega (-\omega \operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\,i-\omega \operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\,j) \\  & =-{\omega }^{2}\cdot R(\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\,j) \\  & =-{\omega }^{2}r\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize,

$$
\mathbf a = -\omega^2 \mathbf r.
$$

Therefore, the acceleration vector acts in the *opposite* direction to $\mathbf r.$ In other words, $\mathbf a$ points *toward the center of the circle*. Moreover, we have

$$
||\mathbf a|| = \omega^2 || \mathbf r ||.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172168 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

Suppose a particle $P$ is initially at the point $(1,0)$ and moves counterclockwise along the unit circle with a fixed **angular velocity** of $\dfrac\pi3$ **radians per second.** 

The first three seconds of the particle's motion are illustrated below.

![](images/00/009b83d5d0e48c6983950a48523838cc569b3a92511dc9362630316b1d88f86b.png)

    

Since the angular velocity is constant, we refer to this as **uniform circular motion**. This fixed angular velocity is denoted $\omega,$ and we write

$$
\omega = \dfrac\pi 3\,\textrm{rad/s}.
$$

Now, let $\mathbf r(t)$ be the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$ Then, we have

$$
\mathbf {r}(t)= \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right) \, \mathbf i + \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right) \,\mathbf j.
$$

It's worth building a picture of why this formula is true:

- We know that $\mathbf r(\theta) = \cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j$ traces out a unit circle, starting at the point $(1,0).$

- We can see from the picture that $P$ will return to the starting position after $t=6$ seconds, so the angular frequency of the motion is

$$
\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi t}{3})\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi t}{3})\,j\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $P$ indeed returns to its starting location when $t=6{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(6) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{6\pi }{3})\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{6\pi }{3})\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)\,j \\  & =r(0).\end{aligned}
$$

In general, if a particle moves counterclockwise along a circle of radius $R$ centered at $O$ with initial position $(R,0),$ then its position vector $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\mathbf {r}(t)= R\left(\cos\omega t \, \mathbf i + \sin\omega t \,\mathbf j\right)\!\,.
$$

Note that for clockwise motion, we have $\omega < 0.$

Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173205 :tutorial/content "Suppose a particle $P$ moves along a circle of radius $R$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. 

![](images/45/4564f4c4fcd8068f3bf1645a310afab7fcdc2f82fec6966cb220558c1e93639a.png)

    

Note the following:

- The **position vector** $\mathbf r$ extends from the origin to $P$ in the *radial* direction, while

- the **velocity vector** $\mathbf v$ points in the direction of the particle's motion, *tangential* to the circle.

First, let's assume that $P$ is at the point $(R,0)$ when $t=0.$ Then, we have

$$
\mathbf r(t) = R\left(\cos\omega t \, \mathbf i + \sin\omega t \,\mathbf j\right).
$$

We can easily derive a convenient formula relating $\mathbf v$ and $\omega$ by differentiating $\mathbf r(t){:}$

Differentiating once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & ={r}^{′}(t) \\  & ={(R(\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\,j))}^{′} \\  & =R\omega (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\,j).\end{aligned}
$$

By computing the magnitude of this vector, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}||v|{|}^{2} & ={R}^{2}{\omega }^{2}((-\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t)^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t)}^{2}) \\  & ={R}^{2}{\omega }^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡\omega t+{cos}^{2}⁡\omega t) \\  & ={R}^{2}{\omega }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Taking the square root, we get

$$
||\mathbf v || = R|\omega|.
$$

Note that while the magnitude of the velocity vector (i.e., the speed) is constant, its direction is continuously changing, which means that an object in uniform circular motion also experiences *acceleration* (more on this shortly)." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173260 :tutorial/content "Let's return to our particle $P$ moving along a circle of radius $R$ centered at the origin in the $xy$ plane.

$$

Differentiating, we get the velocity vector $\mathbf v{:}$ 

$$
\mathbf v(t) =R\omega\left(-\sin\omega t \, \mathbf i + \cos\omega t \,\mathbf j\right)

Differentiating once more, we get an expression for the acceleration vector:

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =(v(t))^{′} \\  & =(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)^{′} \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}||v(t)|| & =\sqrt{(-5\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t)^{2}+(5\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{\pi }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\pi t+25{\pi }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\pi t} \\  & =\sqrt{25{\pi }^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡\pi t+{cos}^{2}⁡\pi t)} \\  & =5\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the object's speed is $5 \pi \textrm{ m/s}.$

Note that the speed is constant, but the velocity is not.

$$
||\mathbf v|| = R|\omega|,
$$

where $R$ is the radius of the circle, and $\omega$ is the angular velocity.

In our case, the radius of the circle is $R=5\,\textrm m$ and the angular frequency $\omega = \pi \,\textrm{rad/s}.$ Therefore,

$$
||\mathbf v|| = 5\cdot |\pi| = 5\pi \textrm{ m/s}.

First, we find the velocity vector by differentiating the position vector. We get

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =(v(t))^{′} \\  & =(-12\operatorname{sin}⁡3t\,i+12\operatorname{cos}⁡3t\,j)^{′} \\  & =-36\operatorname{cos}⁡3t\,i-36\operatorname{sin}⁡3t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}||a(t)|| & =\sqrt{(-36\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)^{2}+(-36\operatorname{sin}⁡3t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{36}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡3t+{36}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡3t} \\  & =\sqrt{{36}^{2}} \\  & =36\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the magnitude of the acceleration is $36\, \textrm{m/s}^2.$

Note that $||\mathbf a||$ is constant, but $\mathbf a$ is not.

**Method 2**

For uniform circular motion in the $xy$-plane, we have

$$
\mathbf a = -\omega^2\mathbf r \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad ||\mathbf a|| = \omega^2||\mathbf r||.
$$

In our case, the radius of the circle is $R=4\,\textrm m$ and the angular frequency $\omega = 3\,\textrm{rad/s}.$ Therefore,

$$
||\mathbf a|| = 3^2\cdot |4| = 36\, \textrm{m/s}^2.

Suppose a particle $P$ is initially at the point $(1,0)$ and moves counterclockwise along the unit circle with a fixed **angular velocity** of $\dfrac\pi3$ **radians per second.** 

The first three seconds of the particle's motion are illustrated below.

![](images/00/009b83d5d0e48c6983950a48523838cc569b3a92511dc9362630316b1d88f86b.png)

Since the angular velocity is constant, we refer to this as **uniform circular motion**. This fixed angular velocity is denoted $\omega,$ and we write

$$
\omega = \dfrac\pi 3\,\textrm{rad/s}.
$$

Now, let $\mathbf r(t)$ be the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$ Then, we have

$$
\mathbf {r}(t)= \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right) \, \mathbf i + \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right) \,\mathbf j.
$$

It's worth building a picture of why this formula is true:

- We know that $\mathbf r(\theta) = \cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j$ traces out a unit circle, starting at the point $(1,0).$

- We can see from the picture that $P$ will return to the starting position after $t=6$ seconds, so the angular frequency of the motion is

$$
\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi t}{3})\,i+\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi t}{3})\,j\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $P$ indeed returns to its starting location when $t=6{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(6) & =\operatorname{cos}(\frac{6\pi }{3})\,i+\operatorname{sin}(\frac{6\pi }{3})\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}(2\pi )\,i+\operatorname{sin}(2\pi )\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}(0)\,i+\operatorname{sin}(0)\,j \\  & =r(0).\end{aligned}
$$

In general, if a particle moves counterclockwise along a circle of radius $R$ centered at $O$ with initial position $(R,0),$ then its position vector $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\mathbf {r}(t)= R\left(\cos\omega t \, \mathbf i + \sin\omega t \,\mathbf j\right)\!\,.
$$

Note that for clockwise motion, we have $\omega < 0.$

:tutorial/content "Suppose a particle $P$ moves along a circle of radius $R$ centered at the origin in the $xy$-plane. 

![](images/45/4564f4c4fcd8068f3bf1645a310afab7fcdc2f82fec6966cb220558c1e93639a.png)

Note the following:

- The **position vector** $\mathbf r$ extends from the origin to $P$ in the *radial* direction, while

- the **velocity vector** $\mathbf v$ points in the direction of the particle's motion, *tangential* to the circle.

First, let's assume that $P$ is at the point $(R,0)$ when $t=0.$ Then, we have

$$
\mathbf r(t) = R\left(\cos\omega t \, \mathbf i + \sin\omega t \,\mathbf j\right).
$$

We can easily derive a convenient formula relating $\mathbf v$ and $\omega$ by differentiating $\mathbf r(t){:}$

Differentiating once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & ={r}^{'}(t) \\  & ={(R(\operatorname{cos}\omega t\,i+\operatorname{sin}\omega t\,j))}^{'} \\  & =R\omega (-\operatorname{sin}\omega t\,i+\operatorname{cos}\omega t\,j).\end{aligned}
$$

By computing the magnitude of this vector, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}||v|{|}^{2} & ={R}^{2}{\omega }^{2}((-\operatorname{sin}\omega t)^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}\omega t)}^{2}) \\  & ={R}^{2}{\omega }^{2}({sin}^{2}\omega t+{cos}^{2}\omega t) \\  & ={R}^{2}{\omega }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Taking the square root, we get

$$
||\mathbf v || = R|\omega|.
$$

Note that while the magnitude of the velocity vector (i.e., the speed) is constant, its direction is continuously changing, which means that an object in uniform circular motion also experiences *acceleration* (more on this shortly)." :tutorial/id #uuid "04a3ea53-9923-588e-b205-6980447b9231" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5805 :tutorial/title "Linear vs. Angular Velocity"} :step/id #uuid "b328c2b2-b79d-5bf1-9c7d-2b99b0ab3382" :step/math-academy-id 35574 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172914}} {:db/id 17592186173094 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173260 :tutorial/content "Let's return to our particle $P$ moving along a circle of radius $R$ centered at the origin in the $xy$ plane.

Once again, let's assume that $P$ is at the point $(R,0)$ when $t=0.$ Then, we have

$$
\mathbf r(t) = R\left(\cos\omega t \, \mathbf i + \sin\omega t \,\mathbf j\right).
$$

Differentiating, we get the velocity vector $\mathbf v{:}$ 

$$
\mathbf v(t) =R\omega\left(-\sin\omega t \, \mathbf i + \cos\omega t \,\mathbf j\right)
$$

Differentiating once more, we get an expression for the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & ={v}^{'}(t) \\  & =R\omega {(-\operatorname{sin}\omega t\,i+\operatorname{cos}\omega t\,j)}^{'} \\  & =R\omega (-\omega \operatorname{cos}\omega t\,i-\omega \operatorname{sin}\omega t\,j) \\  & =-{\omega }^{2}\cdot R(\operatorname{cos}\omega t\,i+\operatorname{sin}\omega t\,j) \\  & =-{\omega }^{2}r\end{aligned}
$$

To summarize,

$$
\mathbf a = -\omega^2 \mathbf r.
$$

Therefore, the acceleration vector acts in the *opposite* direction to $\mathbf r.$ In other words, $\mathbf a$ points *toward the center of the circle*. Moreover, we have

$$
||\mathbf a|| = \omega^2 || \mathbf r ||.

The first three seconds of the particle's motion are illustrated below.

![](images/00/009b83d5d0e48c6983950a48523838cc569b3a92511dc9362630316b1d88f86b.png)

Since the angular velocity is constant, we refer to this as **uniform circular motion**. This fixed angular velocity is denoted $\omega,$ and we write

$$
\omega = \dfrac\pi 3\,\textrm{rad/s}.
$$

Now, let $\mathbf r(t)$ be the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$ Then, we have

$$
\mathbf {r}(t)= \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right) \, \mathbf i + \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right) \,\mathbf j.
$$

It's worth building a picture of why this formula is true:

- We know that $\mathbf r(\theta) = \cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j$ traces out a unit circle, starting at the point $(1,0).$

- We can see from the picture that $P$ will return to the starting position after $t=6$ seconds, so the angular frequency of the motion is

$$
\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi t}{3})\,i+\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi t}{3})\,j\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $P$ indeed returns to its starting location when $t=6{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(6) & =\operatorname{cos}(\frac{6\pi }{3})\,i+\operatorname{sin}(\frac{6\pi }{3})\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}(2\pi )\,i+\operatorname{sin}(2\pi )\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}(0)\,i+\operatorname{sin}(0)\,j \\  & =r(0).\end{aligned}
$$

In general, if a particle moves counterclockwise along a circle of radius $R$ centered at $O$ with initial position $(R,0),$ then its position vector $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\mathbf {r}(t)= R\left(\cos\omega t \, \mathbf i + \sin\omega t \,\mathbf j\right)\!\,.
$$

Note that for clockwise motion, we have $\omega < 0.$
